origin: founder request, 9 Nov 2026 — first run of a new idea under the current skill

defaults.condition: Fail if the problem can't be stated in one sentence an orthopaedic or sports-medicine surgeon would agree with, without mentioning the technology.

defaults.header: Is there one place to start?
defaults.condition: Fail if no single first indication — one population or procedure — can be established. The input named a category, so a candidate table was required.

venture_specific.header: Is the problem serious, and does anyone count it?
venture_specific.condition: Fail if losing meniscal tissue leads to arthritis or another knee operation in fewer than 1 in 20 patients under today's practice, or if no registry, trial, or series has measured what happens to a knee after meniscus is removed.

evidence.default_1: Problem sentence stated without the technology; ESSKA 2016: 'Loss of meniscus function may negatively affect the knee in the long term' (Grade B).
evidence.default_2: Symptomatic meniscus-deficient knee under about 55 (the MAT population), selected from the candidate table.
evidence.venture_specific: Abram 2019 (n=834,393): 13.49% knee arthroplasty within 15 years of partial meniscectomy, RR 10.27 vs general population; Roos 1998: KL≥2 OA 48% vs 7% at 21 years.

sentence.text: When a torn meniscus cannot be repaired, the tissue is removed, and the knee that loses it develops arthritis and comes to replacement at many times the rate of an intact knee. The only tissue replacement in use — a donor meniscus — reaches a tiny fraction of patients, is sized with error, and survives in about three of four patients at ten years and six of ten at fifteen.

first_indication.statement: Patients under about 55 with a symptomatic meniscus-deficient knee after subtotal or total meniscectomy — today's candidates for meniscal allograft transplantation.

q3_how_often_how_bad.number: 13.49% knee arthroplasty within 15 years of partial meniscectomy (16,256/120,493); RR 10.27 vs general population; RR 39.62 at ages 30–39; HR 2.99 vs own other knee
q3_how_often_how_bad.harm_magnitude: Arthritis and arthroplasty, not death. Roos 1998: KL≥2 OA 48% vs 7% at 21 yr after open meniscectomy, RR 14.0. MAT survivorship 73.5% at 10 yr, 60.3% at 15 yr; complication 21.3%, failure 10.6%.
q3_how_often_how_bad.workaround_burden: Donor meniscus: sizing error 7.8% by standard method, >10% by anthropometric methods; irradiation reduces strength; fresh-frozen grafts limited viability; concurrent HTO when malaligned; graft failure 1.8–25% and reoperation 1.6–33% within 5 yr by fixation technique. MAT at 0.12–0.24 per 100,000/yr. Cost: not found. Denominator (symptomatic meniscus-deficient population): not found.

q4_solved_today.standard_of_care: Repair when the tear allows; partial meniscectomy when it does not; MAT for the symptomatic meniscus-deficient knee in a young patient, with HTO when malaligned; non-operative care until arthroplasty.
q4_solved_today.workarounds: Partial synthetic scaffolds in some markets, only with an intact meniscal rim.

evidence.claim: MAT indications and partial scaffold limits
evidence.label: verified

q5_whats_wrong.gap_in_fields_words: ESSKA: 'Loss of meniscus function may negatively affect the knee in the long term'; 'the high risk of osteoarthritis after APM remains a concern'. MAT 'remains underutilized'; 'graft deterioration inevitably occurs at 7 to 10 years'; 'the decision often depends on the surgeon's preference and graft availability'. 'Neither CMI nor Actifit has demonstrated a clear advantage over partial meniscectomy'.

evidence.claim: MAT underutilized; sizing; availability; scaffold statements
evidence.label: verified

evidence.claim: Graft deterioration inevitably occurs at 7 to 10 years
evidence.label: verified

q6_looking_to_change.demand_evidence: Repairs doubled 2005–2011 while meniscectomies flat (Abrams 2013); debridement down, repair up in all age groups 2001–2017 (ABOS 2021); ESSKA 2016 consensus against first-line surgery for degenerative tears; two meniscus implants with FDA Breakthrough designations, one De Novo planned 2026 (BONEZONE Feb 2026) — demand evidence only.
q6_looking_to_change.practice_shift_flag: Gate 8: the shift to repair and away from meniscectomy shrinks the meniscus-deficient population at the margin; irreparable tears not shown to be disappearing.

q7_business_contradiction.note: No contradiction evident; a timing split recorded — the surgeon who removes tissue does not see the arthritis, the arthroplasty surgeon did not remove it, and the payer at 50 may differ from the payer at 35. Who pays at the time of loss is gate 6.

case_against: The most dramatic harm number (48% vs 7%, RR 14) is from open meniscectomy in 1973, a procedure no longer performed; the modern cohort shows 13.49% arthroplasty at 15 years in patients with mean age 50 and degenerative tears, and ESSKA calls the degenerative tear a feature of a knee already at risk — the knee, not the meniscectomy, may be the problem (HR 2.99 vs the other knee blunts but does not settle this). The acute population is tiny as measured (MAT 0.12–0.24 per 100,000, flat for a decade): either rare, or the field has decided to live with it. The field already has a tissue replacement and its main response is upstream — repair more, remove less — which shrinks the population. Most meniscectomy patients are over 50 with degenerative tears for whom the consensus is not to operate first. Nobody has priced the problem.
verdict_reason: Losing meniscal tissue is a real, recognized, counted harm — tenfold arthroplasty risk in a national cohort of 834,393, fortyfold in the young — and the only tissue replacement is rare, hard to size, and expected to deteriorate within a decade by the field's own account. Standard of care does not solve it. The open question is how many people have the acute form; routed to the interviews and gate 3. Harm is arthritis and reoperation, not death.

discovery_kit.sentence_to_test: When a young patient's meniscus can't be repaired you take it out, and you know what that knee looks like in fifteen years — and the only tissue you can put back is a donor meniscus that's hard to size and wears out in a decade.
who_to_talk_to: A sports-medicine orthopaedic surgeon who performs MAT at a center that does them regularly
An orthopaedic surgeon who performs meniscectomy and repair but refers MAT out — the entry point
An arthroplasty surgeon who replaces knees in patients with a meniscectomy history — inherits the consequence
Someone at a musculoskeletal tissue bank who fills meniscal allograft orders — lives with sizing, supply, processing
The person who pays — a payer medical director who approves MAT, or the orthopaedic service-line administrator who absorbs allograft and episode cost
Optional sixth: a patient who had a meniscectomy young and a MAT or knee replacement later

core_questions: Tell me about the last young patient whose meniscus you couldn't save. What did you do, and what did you tell them about their knee's future?
When did you last perform or refer a meniscal transplant? What decided it, and what got in the way?
How do you find out, years later, what happened to the knees you took meniscus out of?
What do you wish you had in the room when a tear turns out to be irreparable?
Who in your institution notices when a 35-year-old comes back for a knee replacement at 50?
disqualifying_findings: Surgeons say the young, symptomatic, meniscus-deficient patient is rare and cannot recall one from the past year.
MAT surgeons say graft supply and sizing are fine and the only limit is that few patients need it.
Nobody can describe a consequence of meniscal loss they personally see; nobody connects the arthritis back.
Everyone says the answer is repair, and that the irreparable tear is vanishing.
Payers who fund the arthroplasty do not connect it to the meniscectomy and see no reason to pay at the time of loss.
pointers: Do not pitch. Do not describe, name, or hint at the technology; if asked, say you are studying the problem first and will share later.
Ask about the last time, not the usual case.
Ask what it cost — in time, money, staff, outcomes — and who paid.
'That sounds interesting' means nothing. A story about a recurring complication with its consequences is a signal.
Let silence work; do not fill it or lead the witness.
Write down their words, not your summary; note which gap each answer closes.

When someone says a step costs nothing, ask who pays for the people and the time it takes. A cost the speaker doesn't feel is usually a cost someone else does — find that person before you strike the gap.
Five conversations are a screen, not a validation; they decide whether the idea earns thirty more.

flags_for_later_gates.flag: Record of meniscal substitutes (allografts, partial scaffolds, polymer implants, tissue-engineered constructs) and the fixation/sizing/processing literature — fatal-flaw review
Size of the meniscus-deficient population is the central unknown: MAT 0.12–0.24 per 100,000; meniscectomies in the hundreds of thousands per year (secondary); no denominator found
Named in sources: Stryker (CMI), Phoenix Kinetics (NUsurface), OrthoPreserve (Defender); tissue banks as incumbent MAT suppliers — recorded, not evaluated
Who pays for MAT today (prior auth, allograft reimbursement in the episode); harm of loss paid 10–20 years later, often by a different payer

Two meniscus implants with FDA Breakthrough designations (2019; Jan 2025); one De Novo planned 2026 after an earlier advisory hearing; a cell- or tissue-based meniscus likely a different pathway — note only
Practice shift: repair rising, debridement falling (2001–2017; 2005–2011); consensus against first-line surgery for degenerative tears; post-meniscectomy population contracting at the margin — track
Team gate — founder background supplied in conversation; not evaluated here
